meta.title: Brazilian elections
sources: Wikipedia: Brazilian presidential and general election articles, 1891–2022, and parliamentary election articles, 1934–1990 (results, infoboxes and leads)
TSE and historical figures as reported there

presEras.label: The Old Republic
presEras.blurb: The First Republic's presidents were chosen on a tiny, literate-male franchise under 'café com leite' arrangements between the big-state machines, with open ballots and routine fraud. The chain broke in 1930, when the defeated Getúlio Vargas took power by revolution instead.

presEras.label: The Vargas era
presEras.blurb: Vargas was confirmed in office indirectly by the Constituent Assembly in 1934; the promised 1938 direct election never came — his Estado Novo coup of 1937 cancelled it and closed the Congress.

presEras.label: The populist republic
presEras.blurb: Democratisation in 1945 brought Brazil's first mass elections: Dutra's win, Vargas's astonishing comeback by direct vote in 1950, Kubitschek's developmentalist 1955 victory, and Jânio Quadros's 1960 landslide — the last direct presidential vote for nearly three decades.

presEras.label: The military regime's electoral college
presEras.blurb: After the 1964 coup, presidents-general were ratified by a purged Congress and later an electoral college, with the imposed ARENA majority guaranteeing the outcome. The 1985 college vote turned the weapon around: the opposition's Tancredo Neves won, and the dictatorship ended.

presEras.label: The New Republic
presEras.blurb: Direct two-round elections returned in 1989 with Collor's win over Lula. The real gave Cardoso two first-round victories, Lula's 2002 breakthrough began four straight Workers' Party wins, and the Bolsonaro years ended with the closest runoff in Brazilian history in 2022. The next contest is due in October 2026.

legEras.label: Constituent assemblies
legEras.blurb: The 1934 Constituent Assembly wrote the short-lived Second Republic's constitution; the 1945 election seated the assembly that wrote 1946's, and 1947 filled the remaining seats — the founding votes of two democratic orders.

legEras.label: The populist republic's Congress
legEras.blurb: Multiparty congressional politics under the 1946 constitution: the PSD, UDN and PTB triangle that framed every presidency from Dutra to Goulart, elected on a franchise that still excluded illiterate Brazilians.

legEras.label: The two-party dictatorship
legEras.blurb: The military regime dissolved the parties and imposed exactly two: the governing ARENA and the tolerated opposition MDB. The MDB's 1974 surge turned a managed safety valve into a genuine opposition — elections the regime counted on winning began to bite.

legEras.label: Abertura and the New Republic
legEras.blurb: The controlled opening restored multiparty contests in 1982, the 1986 election seated the assembly that wrote the 1988 Constitution, and 1990 elected the first Congress of the restored democracy.

presidential.summary: Indirect presidential elections were held in Brazil on 25 February 1891. They were the first presidential elections in the country following the overthrow of the monarchy, with the president and vice president elected by members of Congress.
presidential.caveat: An Old Republic election: a very restricted, literate-male franchise, open voting and machine control make the recorded totals a poor guide to popular opinion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Brazil on 1 March 1918. The presidential elections were won by former President Rodrigues Alves, who received 99% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: An Old Republic election: a very restricted, literate-male franchise, open voting and machine control make the recorded totals a poor guide to popular opinion.

presidential.summary: Early presidential elections were held in Brazil on 13 April 1919, following the death of Rodrigues Alves, who had been elected the previous year. The result was a victory for Epitácio Pessoa of the Paraíba Republican Party (and supported by the Paulista Republican Party and the Mineiro Republican Party), who received 71% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: An Old Republic election: a very restricted, literate-male franchise, open voting and machine control make the recorded totals a poor guide to popular opinion.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Brazil on 1 March 1930. In the presidential elections the result was a victory for Júlio Prestes of the Paulista Republican Party, who received 58% of the vote.
presidential.caveat: An Old Republic election: a very restricted, literate-male franchise, open voting and machine control make the recorded totals a poor guide to popular opinion.

presidential.summary: Indirect presidential elections were held in Brazil on 17 July 1934. Unlike previous elections which had been public (with the exception of the 1891 presidential election), this election was carried out by the Constituent Assembly.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the Constituent Assembly, not a popular election.

presidential.summary: General elections were held in Brazil on 2 December 1945, the first since the establishment of Getúlio Vargas' Estado Novo. The presidential elections were won by Eurico Gaspar Dutra of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), whilst the PSD also won a majority of seats in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

General elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1950. The presidential elections were won by Getúlio Vargas of the Brazilian Labour Party, whilst the Social Democratic Party remained the largest party in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, although they lost their majority in the former.

Presidential elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1955 to elect both the president and vice president. Juscelino Kubitschek of the Social Democratic Party was elected president with 36% of the vote, while João Goulart of the Brazilian Labour Party was elected vice president with 44% of the vote.

presidential.knownAs: The last direct vote for 29 years
presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1960 to elect the president and vice president. Jânio Quadros of the National Labour Party (PTN), heading a coalition of the PTN, the National Democratic Union and the Christian Democratic Party was elected president with 48% of the vote.

Indirect presidential elections were held in Brazil on 11 April 1964 shortly after the 1964 coup carried out by the Brazilian military. Humberto de Alencar Castelo Branco was elected president by the National Congress, receiving 361 of the 366 votes cast.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote under the military regime: the president was ratified by a purged Congress or electoral college, with the outcome guaranteed in advance. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: Indirect presidential elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1966 through an electoral college system. It was the second election during the Brazilian military government, with Artur da Costa e Silva as the sole candidate.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote under the military regime: the president was ratified by a purged Congress or electoral college, with the outcome guaranteed in advance. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: The National Congress had been closed since Institutional Act Number Five was issued on 13 December 1968. President Artur da Costa e Silva left office on 14 October due to ill health, later dying on 17 December.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote under the military regime: the president was ratified by a purged Congress or electoral college, with the outcome guaranteed in advance. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: All elections during the military government elected candidates from the National Renewal Alliance Party (ARENA), though the 1966 and 1969 were one-party elections. In other elections during the military government, there were two parties running for elections.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote under the military regime: the president was ratified by a purged Congress or electoral college, with the outcome guaranteed in advance. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: Indirect presidential elections were held in Brazil on 15 October 1978. The opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) chose an anti-candidate to fill the spot and denounce the restrictive democracy.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote under the military regime: the president was ratified by a purged Congress or electoral college, with the outcome guaranteed in advance. Recorded here as history, not as a free election.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Brazil on 15 January 1985, the last to be held indirectly through an electoral college, and the last to be held under the military regime.
presidential.caveat: An indirect electoral-college vote under the military regime's rules — won, for the first time, by the opposition.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Brazil in 1989, with the first round on November 15 and a second round on December 17. They were the first direct presidential elections since 1960, the first to be held using a two-round system and the first to take place under the 1988 constitution, which followed two decades of authoritarian rule after the 1964 Brazilian coup d'état.

Elected in 1989, President Fernando Collor of the centre-right National Reconstruction Party (PRN) had resigned in the face of an impeachment trial, resulting in Vice President Itamar Franco succeeding him. Facing a fiscal crisis Franco's government launched the Plano Real ("Real Plan") to stabilize the national economy.

General elections were held in Brazil on 4 October 1998 to elect the President, National Congress and state governorships. If no candidate in the presidential election received more than 50% of the vote in the first round, a second-round runoff would have been held on 25 October.

General elections were held in Brazil on 6 October 2002, with a second round of the presidential election on 27 October. The elections were held in the midst of an economic crisis that began in the second term of the incumbent president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso of the centre-right Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB).

Elected by a wide margin in the 2002 presidential elections, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the centre-left Workers' Party (PT) ran for reelection. During his first term in office, Lula implemented a wide array of social programs, including the Fome Zero (Zero Hunger) and Bolsa Família (Family Allowance) programs.
General elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 2010 to elect the president, National Congress and state governors.

General elections were held in Brazil on 5 October 2014 to elect the president, the National Congress, and state governorships. As no candidate in the presidential election received more than 50% of the vote in the first round on 5 October 2014, a second-round runoff was held on 26 October 2014.

General elections were held in Brazil on 7 October 2018 to elect the president, National Congress and state governors. As no candidate in the presidential election (and for the gubernatorial election in some states) received more than 50% of the vote in the first round, a runoff round was held of those offices on 28 October.

General elections were held in Brazil on 2 October 2022 to elect the president, vice president, the National Congress, the governors, vice governors and legislative assemblies of all federative units, and the district council of Fernando de Noronha.

legislative.summary: Following the Revolution of 1930, a constitutional assembly was elected in 1933 and drew up a new constitution, which came into force on 16 July 1934.

General elections were held in Brazil on 2 December 1945, the first since the establishment of Getúlio Vargas' Estado Novo. The presidential elections were won by Eurico Gaspar Dutra of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), whilst the PSD also won a majority of seats in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

Parliamentary elections were held in Brazil on 19 January 1947. The elections were for 19 vacant seats in the Chamber of Deputies, one additional Senator for each state (except Santa Catarina, which elected two), and for all state Governors and legislatures.

General elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1950. The presidential elections were won by Getúlio Vargas of the Brazilian Labour Party, whilst the Social Democratic Party remained the largest party in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, although they lost their majority in the former.

Parliamentary elections were held in Brazil on 15 November 1966. They were the first elections held after a military coup in 1964.
legislative.caveat: Held under the military regime's imposed two-party system; competitive, but on the dictatorship's terms.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Brazil on 15 November 1970. The result was a victory for the National Renewal Alliance Party, which won 223 of the 310 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 40 of the 46 seats in the Senate.
legislative.caveat: Held under the military regime's imposed two-party system; competitive, but on the dictatorship's terms.

legislative.summary: They were the last elections held under a mandatory two-party system, as reforms were enacted in 1979 by Brazil's governing military junta, represented in Congress by ARENA, to allow a multi-party system to emerge in an effort to combat the growing popularity of the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) by splitting their vote.
legislative.caveat: Held under the military regime's imposed two-party system; competitive, but on the dictatorship's terms.

legislative.summary: The pro-government Democratic Social Party (the successor of the ruling National Renewal Alliance) won 235 of the 479 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 15 of the 25 seats in the Senate. Voter turnout was 82% for the Chamber of Deputies and 83% for the Senate.
Parliamentary elections were held in Brazil on 15 November 1986. The Brazilian Democratic Movement Party won 260 of the 487 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 38 of the 49 seats in the Senate.

legislative.knownAs: First Congress of the New Republic
legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Brazil on 3 October 1990, the first held under the 1988 constitution. The Brazilian Democratic Movement Party emerged as the largest party, winning 108 of the 502 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 8 of the 31 seats in the Senate.
